entries.why_wrong: That's not how `||` works — it doesn't evaluate the right operand first based on precedence; it evaluates `config.timeout` first and only reaches `5000` if that value is falsy. So `timeout` isn't 'always 5000', it's whatever was passed in unless that value is falsy, which is exactly the trap: a passed-in `0` is falsy too, so it gets replaced with `5000` even though the caller meant it.

Accessing a property that doesn't exist on an object never throws in JavaScript — `config.timeout` just evaluates to `undefined` when the key is missing. The real problem isn't a crash on missing keys, it's that the fallback logic can't tell `undefined` apart from a deliberately-set `0`, so it overwrites a valid `0` with `5000`.

Adding a `typeof` check wouldn't fix anything here — the value coming in is already a number when it's provided, so type coercion isn't the issue. The actual bug is which values trigger the default: `||` falls back on any falsy value, including a legitimately-set `0`, not just on `null`/`undefined`.
